::: {.visual-intro}
I deliberately worsen next-token prediction in a **target language** to test whether that change can
largely spare a close relative. For German → Dutch, German is the target and Dutch is the language I want
to spare. I make this change by modifying the model's learned weights: a **weight edit**.

Lucius Bushnaq's [Exploration: Fine-Tuning with Parameter Decomposition](https://www.lesswrong.com/posts/ieoWstubDQWLrMnhH/exploration-fine-tuning-with-parameter-decomposition)
showed that changing one subcomponent's coefficient in [Goodfire's four-layer, 67-million-parameter language model](https://www.goodfire.com/research/interpreting-lm-parameters)
could weaken German predictions while largely sparing French and Spanish. I use the same model and
decomposition to test three pairs of close relatives: German/Dutch, Spanish/Portuguese and French/Italian.
:::

## Edit one rank-one subcomponent

To make a targeted weight change, I select one subcomponent from
[Goodfire's adVersarial Parameter Decomposition (VPD)](https://www.goodfire.com/research/interpreting-lm-parameters)
and adjust its contribution. VPD writes a weight matrix $W$ as a sum of **rank-one subcomponents** plus a
residual. The decomposition is trained so that few subcomponents are needed on any input. Each subcomponent $A$ is the outer
product of an output vector $u_{\mathrm{out}}$ and an input vector $v_{\mathrm{in}}$:

$$
A = u_{\mathrm{out}}v_{\mathrm{in}}^\top.
$$

For an input $x$, the input vector reads out one number, $v_{\mathrm{in}}^\top x$. The output vector determines
the direction in which that number contributes to the matrix's output:

$$
Ax = u_{\mathrm{out}}\bigl(v_{\mathrm{in}}^\top x\bigr).
$$

The edit changes a single number, the selected subcomponent's coefficient $c$:

$$
W_{\mathrm{edited}} = (W-A) + cA.
$$

Changing this coefficient changes many entries of the weight matrix. The subcomponent's two vectors stay
fixed, as do all other subcomponents and the residual. At $c=1$ the matrix is unchanged.
$c=0$ removes the selected contribution, and $c<0$ reverses its sign. The slider below illustrates this operation
on a toy matrix.

## Comparing ways to change the weights

I compare the VPD edit with three other ways to change the weights, all aimed at worsening target-language
prediction while preserving English predictions.

**Rank-one LoRA** learns its own output and input vectors in the same weight matrix:

$$
\Delta W_{\mathrm{LoRA}} = a_{\mathrm{out}}b_{\mathrm{in}}^\top.
$$

This lets LoRA choose a different direction while keeping the update's rank and the edited matrix fixed.

**Full-matrix fine-tuning** gives the learned update more freedom: it can change every entry in the model's
24 attention and feed-forward weight matrices.

The **neuron edit** selects neurons by how much more often they activate on target text than on English
text, then scales their output weights.

The VPD rule ranks subcomponents by their estimated target effect
relative to their English effect. LoRA and full-matrix fine-tuning penalize changes to the original model's
English predictions during training.

These selection and training steps use no Dutch, Portuguese or Italian text. Those languages test whether
the methods also spare a close relative that they were not explicitly trained to preserve.

## Matching the intended damage

To compare side effects fairly, I first make each method worsen the target language by a similar amount.
Otherwise, a method might spare Dutch simply because it barely changed German.

I **calibrate** each edit by adjusting its strength on target-language validation text. I use two targets:
an increase of **0.5 or 1 nat/token** in average prediction loss (cross-entropy) relative to the original model.

I use **Europarl v7**, a corpus of European Parliament proceedings. After calibration, I measure the damage
to both languages on separate text from **58 session dates**.

Across all three pairs and both strengths, the VPD changes largely spared the related language: its average
loss rose by only **0.0003–0.0053 nat/token**. Each of these six changes in this model caused less
related-language damage than rank-one LoRA, full-matrix fine-tuning or the neuron edit.

## English, innit? {#what-changed-in-english}

**Rank-one LoRA and full-matrix fine-tuning preserved the original model's English predictions more
closely** than the VPD changes did. Prediction loss scores the probability of the actual next token.
KL divergence compares probabilities over all possible next tokens before and after the edit.
Lower KL means the English predictions stayed closer to the original model.

```{=html}
<figure class="visual-figure" aria-labelledby="visual-english-caption">
  <div id="visual-english-interactive" hidden>
    <div class="visual-controls">
      <label for="visual-english-pair">Language being changed
        <select id="visual-english-pair"><option value="de">German</option><option value="es">Spanish</option><option value="fr">French</option></select>
      </label>
      <fieldset class="visual-dose"><legend>Target loss increase on validation text</legend>
        <button type="button" data-visual-tau="0.5" aria-pressed="false">0.5 nat/token</button>
        <button type="button" data-visual-tau="1" aria-pressed="true">1 nat/token</button>
      </fieldset>
    </div>
    <div class="visual-chart-pair">
      <div id="visual-english-chart"></div>
    </div>
  </div>
  <div id="visual-english-fallback">
    <p>The VPD edits' English KL is below 0.001 nat/token for every language and strength. Both learned methods have lower English KL in all 18 comparisons. The <a href="index.html#sec-english">paper's English comparison</a> includes the values for all four methods.</p>
  </div>
  <figcaption id="visual-english-caption">English predictions after editing the selected language, measured on the same 58 evaluation dates. Points and ranges show results from the three training subsets. The horizontal scale is logarithmic: each tick is ten times the previous value. KL is measured from the original distribution to the edited one. Zero would mean identical distributions.</figcaption>
</figure>
```

On the evaluated English text, the VPD edits changed next-token probabilities **little on average**:
mean KL stayed below **0.001 nat/token** for every language and strength. For a sense of scale, changing
a two-outcome distribution from **50%/50% to 52%/48%** gives KL ≈ **0.00080**, close to the German VPD
edit's 0.00077 at the 1 nat/token target. This is an illustration of scale, not a measured change of two
percentage points for each token. Individual contexts can change more than the average suggests.

```{=html}
<details class="visual-details">
  <summary>Measurement details and study limits</summary>
  <p>A nat is a unit of information based on natural logarithms. Loss increases are measured relative to the unedited model.</p>
  <p>The evaluation tests six fixed weight changes on new text in one model. Those dates were not used to select or calibrate the changes. Earlier development had used related-language text and identified the German subcomponent, so the selection history was not blind.</p>
  <p>Each text window contains 257 tokens, giving 256 next-token predictions. LoRA and full-matrix fine-tuning use 200 training steps per subset and yield three updates each. All three subsets select the same VPD subcomponent and produce the same scaled edit. Three target languages at two calibrated strengths give six fixed subcomponent edits.</p>
  <p>All 18 simultaneous 95% intervals for the related-language differences lie below zero. These comparisons share the six fixed subcomponent edits, each compared with three methods.</p>
  <p>Intervals describe variation across the 58 session dates for each fixed edit. The edits, training seeds, subcomponents, languages and model stay fixed during resampling. Negative related-language differences favour the subcomponent edit.</p>
  <div id="visual-uncertainty"><p>The <a href="index.html#sec-contrasts">paper's comparison figure</a> gives all simultaneous 95% intervals and the achieved target-effect checks.</p></div>
  <p>Calibration matched validation effects. A separate, post hoc check counted agreement on the evaluation dates only if the entire simultaneous 95% interval for the target-effect difference lay within ±0.1 nat/token. This band was chosen after the results: 15 of 18 comparisons met the criterion. The three exceptions had larger mean target effects for the subcomponent edit, but their mean gaps were still inside the band. One interval also allows a smaller effect. The target-gap intervals use a separate simultaneous family.</p>
</details>
```
